https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: Bob Montgomery, a charity cyclist who recently finished a 5,200km bike ride from Broome to Bowral, died on Monday at the age of 82. His family confirmed his death on social media, saying he had died unexpectedly just a day after completing the cycling feat as a fundraiser for motor neurone disease, alongside his grandson, Tom. They wrote: This was Bob’s sixth interstate fundraising ride in support of Motor Neurone Disease NSW, raising vital funds and awareness for a cause that was deeply personal to him. Fittingly, and now poignantly, the ride was named One Last Ride. At 82 years of age, Bob was still passionately sharing his message only hours before his passing. MND NSW shared a tribute saying the body was “deeply saddened” by the sudden passing, calling Montgomery a “cherished friend and tireless supporter of MND NSW”. https://www.breitbart.com/national-secur.text: KYIV, Ukraine (AP) – Russia launched an intense barrage of ballistic missiles and drones overnight into Saturday, killing at least nine people and wounding 30 civilians in the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, authorities said. The strikes follow a major Russian attack two days earlier that killed at least 10 people and wounded more than 50 others across Ukraine, as Moscow apparently looks to exploit Kyiv´s critical shortage of Western-supplied anti-ballistic missile defenses. The relentless cycle of attacks dims the potential of reaching a diplomatic end to Russia´s more than 4-year-old invasion of its neighbor. Russia’s defense ministry said Saturday it had launched a “massive strike” against “Ukrainian military-industrial complex facilities and logistics centers in Kyiv.” A five-story residential building in the city’s Solomianskyi District was damaged by falling debris and a fire broke out. Rescue workers evacuated 35 people from the upper floors of the building and two people died, with eight reported injured, including two children, according to Ukraine´s state emergency service. In the Darnytskyi District of Kyiv, seven people were killed and another 14 injured after the attack caused fires and damage to houses, vehicles, an administrative and non-residential building, the emergency services said. Elsewhere, emergency workers extinguished a fire in a non-residential building in the capital´s Shevchenkivskyi district. There was no additional information about earlier reports by the district mayor that people were trapped in another residential building. Damage to commercial and residential buildings was reported in two other city districts. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has pressed the United States and other Western partners over Ukraine’s need for more Patriot anti-ballistic missile defense systems to counter missile attacks from Russia. “Every package of ballistic missile interceptors saves the lives of our people. And every night without them results in more casualties,” he wrote on X following the latest attacks. The Ukrainian leader late Friday said he spoke to U.S. Vice President JD Vance and discussed a meeting with President Donald Trump earlier this week in Washington, which Zelenskyy described as “positive and productive.” “The Russian air strikes on our country continue and air defense, specifically interceptors for Patriot systems against ballistic missiles, remains a top priority,” Zelenskyy said Friday in a post on Telegram. At a NATO summit in Ankara in July, Trump said the U.S. would give Ukraine a license to make Patriot systems, but he appeared to move away from that commitment on Friday during a Cabinet meeting at the presidential retreat in Camp David, Maryland, saying he had not yet made a final decision on the matter. From a basement shelter where she was taking cover as a second air alarm sounded for another wave, Liudmyla Nakonechna, 64, described how she was woken by loud explosions at 1:30 a.m. “I ran into the corridor and was standing there when the bathroom door was blown off its hinges and struck me in the leg,” said Nakonechna, whose health is poor after undergoing cancer treatment. “I heard the sound of shattering glass. My balcony was covered in glass and it was completely blown apart, while the windows in my bedroom were also blown out.” Nakonechna had not taken cover in a shelter since Russia’s full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, but the stress became too much, she said. “It’s getting worse by the day,” Nakonechna said. “Whereas before there was an attack once every two weeks, or maybe once a week, now it happens practically every day. It is incredibly hard to bear this psychologically.” Lithuania´s foreign minister said the country’s embassy in Kyiv was damaged when missiles struck nearby overnight. Meanwhile, in Russian-occupied Crimea, the Moscow-appointed head of the city of Sevastopol, Mikhail Razvozhayev, said Saturday that a 60-year-old woman was killed and two other people wounded in a drone attack on the city. https://nineoclock.ro/childhood-shared-w.text: ABOUT US NINE O’CLOCK STAFF 2024 COMMERCIAL OFFER – 2026 Subscribe to the Nine O’Clock 2026 CONTACT Special price offer 2026 with a 50% discount Children Feature in More Than One-Third of Parents’ Social Media Posts Bucharest, 18 August 2026 – Nearly one in three Romanian children aged 9 to 16 has asked their parents to remove content posted about them online, according to EU Kids Online data highlighted in 202. Romania recorded the highest percentage in the comparison, at 29%, while Lithuania ranked at the opposite end, with only 3% of children reporting that they had asked their parents to remove such content. In most of the countries surveyed, up to one-third of children said their parents had posted something about them without first asking for their permission. 29% of Romanian children have asked their parents to remove photos, videos or other content shared about them – the highest percentage in the European comparison presented by the European Commission. A study published in March 2026 found that more than seven out of parents’ 20 most recent social media posts featured at least one of their children. Parents sharing content about their children on social media has been linked to increased family conflict, particularly when the content is posted on TikTok and YouTube. These findings offer a different perspective on digital safety. The conversation typically focuses on how much time children spend online, the inappropriate content they may encounter or the strangers they may interact with. However, research suggests that a child’s first breach of digital privacy may occur within the family itself , when parents begin shaping their child’s online identity before the child is able to decide what they want to make public. Seven in 20 Posts Feature Children The scale of the phenomenon is further highlighted by a 2026 study [ii] involving 470 parents who share content about their children online. On average, more than seven of their 20 most recent posts featured at least one of their children . For adults, photos and videos can be a way to preserve memories, share important moments or stay connected with family and friends. For children, however, the same post can mean losing control over their own image, having a private moment exposed or acquiring a digital identity they did not choose. The study identifies a complex relationship between sharenting and family dynamics. Sharing content featuring children was associated both with a greater sense of closeness reported by parents and with increased parent–child conflict, particularly when children appeared in content posted on TikTok or YouTube. The Child’s Right to Say “No” The perspective of Isabelle Filliozat, one of Europe’s leading authorities on positive parenting, emotional development and trauma-informed approaches , places respect for children, attention to their needs and recognition of the boundaries they express at the heart of this conversation. “Children want to do what is right. They want to behave well. As long as they are respected, they will show respect in return,” says Isabelle Filliozat [iii] . Applied to the digital space, this principle means that parents should not treat their child’s image as content they alone have the right to control. Asking for permission before posting, explaining where the photo will appear, respecting the child’s refusal and removing the content if the child no longer feels comfortable are all ways for adults to show that the child’s voice and boundaries matter. In this context, digital consent becomes a tangible expression of respect within the parent–child relationship, as well as one of the first lessons through which children learn that they have the right to protect their image and privacy. Isabelle Filliozat will make her first appearance in Romania at ParentED Fest , taking place on 17–18 October 2026 at the Aula Magna of the National University of Science and Technology POLITEHNICA Bucharest. Her talk will explore parent–child relationships, emotional development and the challenges facing families in an increasingly digital world. This year’s edition of the parenting festival will bring together seven internationally renowned experts in child psychology and education: Alfie Kohn; Erica Komisar , making her first appearance in Romania; Isabelle Filliozat , also appearing in Romania for the first time; Dr Tina Payne Bryson; Dr Dan Siegel , returning by popular demand; Caroline Welch; and Jessica Joelle Alexander , returning to ParentED Fest for the second time. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Justin Tang JDT Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save OTTAWA - As European countries warn of the emerging threat of Russian hybrid attacks on NATO members helping Ukraine, the Liberal government is watching what it says about potential new security risks. Prime Minister Mark Carney said the threat of hybrid attacks has been "high" for some time now but he opted against wading into a security debate taking shape in Europe. "We're in complete and open conversation with our European allies, our Five Eyes partners, about those threats," Carney told a news conference at the United Nations on Tuesday when asked about the issue by The Canadian Press. "We have extreme vigilance and will continue to be the case. I'm not going to comment on day-to-day shifts in that, though." Hybrid attacks are those that fall under the threshold of traditional warfare, such as cyber operations and acts of sabotage aimed at throwing adversaries off-balance. Earlier Tuesday, Defence Minister David McGuinty said he's taking a "cautious" approach to drawing conclusions from the available intelligence. Asked by The Canadian Press if he's concerned about warnings from Europe about Russia's next moves, the minister said Ottawa is watching the situation closely. "I'm very cautious about what conclusions to draw at this stage. It's very difficult to assimilate all the data," McGuinty said in a brief scrum after delivering a speech to the Canadian Club of Ottawa. The defence minister also said there is "no doubt" that hybrid warfare is "on the expansion" due to countries like Russia, which he said has engaged in some "extremely unacceptable conduct." In recent days, some NATO members have issued warnings and taken precautions in anticipation of Russian attacks. Late last week, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned the public the Kremlin might be planning to hit NATO countries with drones or missiles and to claim the attacks were accidental. French President Emmanuel Macron summoned other party leaders in France for a closed-door intelligence briefing Friday and rolled out new measures to protect critical infrastructure, including defence sites. Lithuania’s president said intelligence assessments suggest Russia is planning attacks on energy and transport infrastructure in Baltic states or Poland. Russia has dismissed such claims as justification for NATO's military buildup. When Norway's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store was in Ottawa on Sunday, he said the warnings from NATO members should be taken seriously but also cautioned against overestimating the threat. “We have in our open assessments of intelligence threats against Norway that there are real threats coming from hybrid activity, ranging all the way to potential sabotage," Store told a joint news conference with Carney on Sunday. "But I would add, let not that become a frenzy — that you see that threat at every corner — because sometimes it may be played up in a way which is not corresponding with realities." On Sunday, Jonatan Vseviov, Estonia's secretary general of foreign affairs, said there has been "a lot of panic on social media lately" about Baltic security. He said in a social media post that if there was any reason to believe an attack is imminent, governments would make that clear. In recent weeks, Denmark accused a Russian ship of shooting flares at a Danish helicopter and Italian jets downed a drone over Lithuanian airspace. Germany has also blamed Russia for a drone attack on an airport in Leipzig last month; an explosive drone was discovered near Ukrainian cargo planes after it failed to detonate. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has proposed a new continental security forum that could better respond to hybrid threats that fall short of acts of war, and which could include Canada as a partner. On Saturday, outgoing chair of the NATO military committee Admiral Giuseppe Cavo Dragone said Russia has been testing the alliance's resolve in recent weeks and months. Dragone said Moscow's behaviour has been reckless, citing recent aerospace violations, drone incidents and other hybrid activities. "We cannot ignore this. The threat is real," he said. "But I want to be clear. These attempts are not dividing us. They are sharpening our tools, making us more united and determined." At the annual NATO summit this past summer, Carney announced an extension of the Canadian-led mission in Latvia until 2031. He also announced Canada will shore up its deployment there by boosting the troop count to around 2,600. McGuinty thanked the family members of the 2,000 troops in Latvia. "This is an important forward-operating location. It's a very important moment for Canada and the multinational brigade that Canada leads there."
